name: Velero
summary: A Kubernetes backup and restore system that turns selected cluster resources and persistent-volume data into object-storage-backed backups and reconstructs them through ordered, plugin-mediated restore workflows.

features.name: Controller-driven backup and restore workflows
features.description: Velero exposes Backup and Restore custom resources and uses controllers to observe them, execute work, and record phases and errors. The server therefore coordinates backup and restore as asynchronous Kubernetes workflows rather than as one blocking client operation.
benefits: Makes long-running backup and restore state inspectable through Kubernetes resources
Allows retries and progress reporting to be separated from the CLI client
Supports scheduled backups through the same resource-oriented control path
costs: Completion is asynchronous and callers must observe resource status
Retries and partial failures require reconciliation and operational cleanup
Kubernetes API availability becomes part of the workflow control path

features.name: Object-storage-backed resource archives
features.description: Velero writes backup metadata and Kubernetes resource data through a BackupStorageLocation abstraction to object storage. The backup controller selects resources and records the backup contents separately from the Kubernetes API server's live state.
benefits: Keeps recovery artifacts outside the source cluster's control-plane storage
Supports cloud-provider and on-premises object-storage implementations through a location boundary
Makes backup contents portable for migration and disaster recovery
costs: Recovery depends on credentials, availability, and compatibility of the object store
Backup retention and artifact lifecycle require separate storage policy
A successful archive does not by itself guarantee application-consistent data

features.name: Ordered plugin-mediated data restore
features.description: The restore controller reconstructs Kubernetes resources in a defined order and delegates provider-specific operations such as volume snapshots and item actions to plugins. Restore ordering and plugin results form explicit boundaries around the generic restore workflow.
benefits: Allows dependent Kubernetes resources to be recreated in a predictable sequence
Supports provider-specific persistent-volume and resource handling without hard-coding every backend
Makes extension behavior observable as restore item results and warnings
costs: Ordering cannot encode every application-level dependency
Plugin availability and version compatibility constrain recoverability
Partial restores can leave a cluster in a mixed state requiring reconciliation

mathematical_views.model: Asynchronous backup and restore state machine
mathematical_views.question: How do Kubernetes backup and restore resources move from requested intent through processing, completion, or failure?
assumptions: Backup and Restore custom resources are the modeled workflow intents
Controller phases summarize progress but do not represent every internal operation
The model treats object storage and plugins as external transition participants

mathematical_views.model: Typed resource dependency graph with archival boundary
mathematical_views.question: Which selected resources, archive objects, volume data, and restore operations must be connected for recovery?
assumptions: Kubernetes resources and persistent-volume data are distinct node classes
BackupStorageLocation and provider plugins are boundary nodes rather than interchangeable storage
Edges express workflow dependency or data transfer and do not prove application consistency

benefits: Inspectable, retryable orchestration for long-running recovery work
costs: Eventual completion and reconciliation require status-aware operators

benefits: Artifacts survive loss of the source cluster and can support migration
costs: External storage credentials, retention, and availability become recovery dependencies

benefits: Provider-specific recovery integrates with a common ordered restore pipeline
costs: Plugin and ordering boundaries cannot guarantee complete application-level recovery
